relationships.description: Shipping the feature produces the stated stakeholder benefit, so the value statement (e.g. 'saves customers ten minutes per order') is the justification for building that piece of user-facing functionality.
relationships.evidence: The feature's spec, PRD or backlog item cites the value statement in its rationale or benefit hypothesis, ideally backed by an analytics or outcome metric attributed to the feature.

relationships.description: The dependent feature cannot work or be released until the prerequisite feature exists, as when an 'export report' screen relies on a 'saved filters' feature being available.
relationships.evidence: A 'blocked by' or 'depends on' link between the two feature tickets in the backlog tool, or a feature flag configuration that requires the prerequisite flag to be enabled.

relationships.description: The feature is the concrete product functionality through which customers actually receive the externally visible business service, such as a 'submit claim' screen that delivers Claims Handling.
relationships.evidence: The service catalogue or the feature's spec maps the feature as a delivery channel for the named business service, and the service's customer journey documentation walks through the feature's screens or commands.

relationships.description: The feature is one of the deliverable units that makes the abstract product ability real, so that delivering it gives the product the stated capability (e.g. a 'card checkout' feature realizing Payment processing).
relationships.evidence: The capability map or roadmap lists the feature under the capability as a child epic or realizing item, and the capability's acceptance is tracked against completion of its features.

relationships.description: The feature's implemented behaviour meets the 'shall/must' statement and its acceptance criteria, making the feature the point where the requirement is fulfilled in the product.
relationships.evidence: A traceability matrix or requirement-to-ticket link connects the requirement ID to the feature, and the feature's acceptance tests verify the requirement's acceptance criteria.

relationships.description: The feature is committed to the scope of the release, version or roadmap phase and is expected to ship by that milestone's target date.
relationships.evidence: The feature ticket's fix-version, release or milestone field names the milestone, or the release plan or roadmap document lists the feature in that milestone's scope.

relationships.description: The feature is designed for the persona's goals and pain points, so the persona is the intended user who perceives and invokes it.
relationships.evidence: The feature's user stories are written as 'As <persona>…', or its design brief and UX research artefacts name the persona as its target user.

relationships.description: The feature relies on an existing product capability it does not itself provide, as when a 'find past orders' screen draws on the Full-text search capability.
relationships.evidence: The feature's design or technical spec lists the capability as a dependency, and its implementation calls the components or services that realize that capability.

notes: delivers-value (traceability) and delivers/supports from motivation overlap; acceptable. The feature→capability uses edge risks confusion with realizes; editors should require that a feature not both realize and use the same capability. realizes→businessservice is plausible but cross-layer; application services usually realize business services, so this may be redundant via capability.
